Mike Trivisonno (September 20, 1947 – October 28, 2021) was an American radio broadcaster, known for hosting his own self-titled afternoon talk show on Cleveland radio station WTAM AM 1100.
Mike Trivisonno: He was widely referred to simply as "Triv" by callers and the Cleveland media.
Mike Trivisonno: He was a frequent caller on the "Sportsline" radio show on WTAM AM 1100 (during this period the station was operating under the WWWE call letters).
Mike Trivisonno: The show was hosted by the acerbic Pete Franklin and dealt with Cleveland sports.
Mike Trivisonno: Franklin, who would typically cut off most callers, began giving "Mike from Mayfield" some latitude due to knowledgeable commentary, particularly regarding the Cleveland Browns.
Mike Trivisonno: Franklin began mockingly referring to Trivisonno as "Mr. Know It All," a moniker he would carry into his own radio career.

Mike Trivisonno: Trivisonno eventually began his own broadcasting career in 1987, working for a time at WNCX, commenting on sports (particularly boxing) and becoming a full-time personality from 1989–1992.
Mike Trivisonno: He began hosting "Sportsline" on WWWE in 1994.
Mike Trivisonno: At first, the show aired from 6-11 p.m.
Mike Trivisonno: The show did well
Mike Trivisonno: in the ratings, even though it was usually up against Cleveland Indians games on WKNR.

Mike Trivisonno: It did so well, the decision was made to put Trivisonno in afternoon drive-time (under the "Sportsline" banner until 1998; under his own name since) ultimately leaving "Sportsline" to other hosts.
Mike Trivisonno: Throughout the program's history, "The Mike Trivisonno Show" was usually either first or second in ratings in its time slot in the market.

Mike Trivisonno: His show had been originally dedicated mostly to sports, but over time became a forum for discussing sports, politics, local issues, current events, or whatever else was on Trivisonno's mind at the time.
Mike Trivisonno: He discussed topics (and frequently argued) with listeners who called in to the show and/or with his various producers and sidekicks that worked alongside him.

Joey D. Vieira: Vieira borrowed the professional surname from his aunt, Ruby Keeler, star of numerous Warner Bros. musicals in the 1930s.

Joey D. Vieira: Film appearances include "The Private War of Major Benson" (1955) with Charlton Heston and "The Patriot" (2000) with Mel Gibson in which he played as Peter Howard.
Joey D. Vieira: Vieira has also written, produced and directed.

Virginia Valli (died September 24, 1968) was an American stage and film actress whose motion picture career started in the silent film era and lasted until the beginning of the sound film era of the 1930s.
Virginia Valli: Born Virginia McSweeney in Chicago, Illinois, she got her acting start in Milwaukee with a stock company.
Virginia Valli: She also did some film work with Essanay Studios in Chicago, starting in 1916.
Virginia Valli: Valli continued to appear in films throughout the 1920s.
Virginia Valli: She was an established star at the Universal studio by the mid-1920s.
Virginia Valli: In 1924 she was the female lead in King Vidor's southern gothic "Wild Oranges", a film now recovered from film vault obscurity.
Virginia Valli: She also appeared in the romantic comedy, "Every Woman's Life", about "the man she could have married, the man she should have married and the man she DID marry."

Virginia Valli: Most of her films were made between 1924 and 1927, and included Alfred Hitchcock's debut feature, "The Pleasure Garden" (1925), "Paid to Love" (1927), with William Powell, and "Evening Clothes" (1927), which featured Adolphe Menjou.
Virginia Valli: Valli performed in "The Man Who Found Himself" with Thomas Meighan.
Virginia Valli: Her first sound picture was "The Isle of Lost Ships" with Jason Robards Sr. and Noah Beery Sr. in 1929.
Virginia Valli: Her last film was in "Night Life in Reno", in 1931.
Virginia Valli: Valli was first married to George Lamson and the two shared a bungalow in Hollywood, near the Hollywood Hotel.
Virginia Valli: In 1931, she married her second husband, actor Charles Farrell.
Virginia Valli: They moved to Palm Springs, where she was a social fixture for many years.
Virginia Valli: She suffered a stroke in 1966, and died two years later, aged 73, in Palm Springs.
Virginia Valli: She was buried in the Welwood Murray Cemetery of that city.
Virginia Valli: She had no children.

Vincenzo Tusa (12 July 1920 – 5 March 2009) was an Italian archeologist.
Vincenzo Tusa: After studying in Mistretta, Tusa graduated in Literature in Catania in 1944 and became an assistant in Archeology.
Vincenzo Tusa: He was hired by the Superintendency of Antiquities in Bologna and two years later he was transferred to Palermo.
Vincenzo Tusa: In 1963 he assumed the post of Superintendent for the BBCC of western Sicily.
Vincenzo Tusa: Tusa promoted excavations in the archaeological sites of Soluntum, Segesta, Selinunte, Motya, Marsala.
Vincenzo Tusa: In the 60's Tusa was the promoter of the "Sicilia Archeologica" magazine.
Vincenzo Tusa: From 1964 to 1991 he was also professor of Punic Antiquities at the Faculty of Letters of the University of Palermo.
Vincenzo Tusa: He was a member of the Accademia dei Lincei in the Moral Sciences class for the Archeology category.
Vincenzo Tusa: His son Sebastiano Tusa, also an archaeologist, was head of the Superintendency for the Sea of the Sicilian Region.

Jean Daullé (18 May 1703 – 23 April 1763) was a French engraver.
Jean Daullé: He was the son of Jean Daullé, a silversmith, and his wife, Anne née Dennel.
Jean Daullé: At the age of fourteen, he received training from an engraver named Robart, at the priory of Saint-Pierre d'Abbeville.
Jean Daullé: He then went to Paris, and worked at the studios of Robert Hecquet (1693-1775), who was also originally from Picardy.
Jean Daullé: In 1735, his work attracted the attention of the engraver and merchant, Pierre-Jean Mariette, who provided him with professional recommendations.
Jean Daullé: Soon after, he was approached by the painter, Hyacinthe Rigaud, who wanted to make him his official engraver.
Jean Daullé: In 1742, Daullé was received at the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture, with his presentation, "Hyacinthe Rigaud Painting his Wife", after a work by Rigaud.
Jean Daullé: He was also admitted as a member of the academy in Augsbourg.
Jean Daullé: Eventually named "Engraver to the King",
Jean Daullé: he trained the future publisher and print dealer, Pierre-François Basan, as well as the German engraver Jean-Georges Wille.
Jean Daullé: Around 1745, he married Gabrielle-Anne Landry and they had five children.
Jean Daullé: Overwhelmed by his large family, his work suffered.

Mike Trivisonno (September 20, 1947 – October 28, 2021) was an American radio broadcaster, known for hosting his own self-titled afternoon talk show on Cleveland radio station WTAM AM 1100.
Mike Trivisonno: He was widely referred to simply as "Triv" by callers and the Cleveland media.
Mike Trivisonno: He was a frequent caller on the "Sportsline" radio show on WTAM AM 1100 (during this period the station was operating under the WWWE call letters).
Mike Trivisonno: The show was hosted by the acerbic Pete Franklin and dealt with Cleveland sports.
Mike Trivisonno: Franklin, who would typically cut off most callers, began giving "Mike from Mayfield" some latitude due to knowledgeable commentary, particularly regarding the Cleveland Browns.
Mike Trivisonno: Franklin began mockingly referring to Trivisonno as "Mr. Know It All," a moniker he would carry into his own radio career.

Mike Trivisonno: Trivisonno eventually began his own broadcasting career in 1987, working for a time at WNCX, commenting on sports (particularly boxing) and becoming a full-time personality from 1989–1992.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Irene Tordoff Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie, DBE (née Fennell; born 29 April 1942 in Fife, Scotland), known as Rennie Fritchie, is a British crossbench peer.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Irene Tordoff Fennell, daughter of Mr and Mrs Charles Frederick Fennell, was educated at Ribston Hall Grammar School for Girls in Gloucester and has had a long career specialising in training and development.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Now described as a "portfolio" worker, she has held various positions including Commissioner for Public Appointments from 1999 to 2005, and President of the Pennell Initiative for Women's Health in Later Life.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: In the 1970s, she was one of the first full-time women's training advisers and pioneered the training of staff in the then new Equal Opportunities Commission.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Using a German Marshall Fellowship awarded in 1985, she drew lessons from the United States of America for the United Kingdom for programmes to improve the status of women.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: She has published extensively on these topics and contributes regularly on them to programmes on television and radio.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: She became Chairman of Nominet in 2010.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: She holds a number of positions outside government.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: She holds an honorary Professorship in Creative Leadership at York University and is Pro-Chancellor at Southampton University, a Civil Service Commissioner and Vice-Chair of the Stroud and Swindon Building Society.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Active in a number of charities, Fritchie has been awarded honorary degrees by a number of academic institutions.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Fritchie is Chair of the 2gether NHS Foundation Trust in Gloucestershire, and in 2012 was appointed as the new chancellor of the University of Gloucestershire.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: In 1960 she married Don Jamie Fritchie with whom she had two children, the elder dying in 1991.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: She was widowed in 1992.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Fritchie became a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in the 1996 New Year Honours.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: On 31 May 2005 she was made a life peer as Baroness Fritchie, of Gloucester in the County of Gloucestershire, and she sits as a crossbencher in the House of Lords.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Irene Tordoff Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie, DBE (née Fennell; born 29 April 1942 in Fife, Scotland), known as Rennie Fritchie, is a British crossbench peer.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Irene Tordoff Fennell, daughter of Mr and Mrs Charles Frederick Fennell, was educated at Ribston Hall Grammar School for Girls in Gloucester and has had a long career specialising in training and development.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Now described as a "portfolio" worker, she has held various positions including Commissioner for Public Appointments from 1999 to 2005, and President of the Pennell Initiative for Women's Health in Later Life.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: In the 1970s, she was one of the first full-time women's training advisers and pioneered the training of staff in the then new Equal Opportunities Commission.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Using a German Marshall Fellowship awarded in 1985, she drew lessons from the United States of America for the United Kingdom for programmes to improve the status of women.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: She has published extensively on these topics and contributes regularly on them to programmes on television and radio.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: She became Chairman of Nominet in 2010.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: She holds a number of positions outside government.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: She holds an honorary Professorship in Creative Leadership at York University and is Pro-Chancellor at Southampton University, a Civil Service Commissioner and Vice-Chair of the Stroud and Swindon Building Society.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Active in a number of charities, Fritchie has been awarded honorary degrees by a number of academic institutions.
Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie: Fritchie is Chair of the 2gether NHS Foundation Trust in Gloucestershire, and in 2012 was appointed as the new chancellor of the University of Gloucestershire.

Hibo Wardere is a Somali-born campaigner against female genital mutilation (FGM), author, and public speaker.

Hibo Wardere: She currently resides in Walthamstow, London, where she worked as a mediator and a regular FGM educator for Waltham Forest Borough.

Hibo Wardere was born in Somalia.
Hibo Wardere: At the age of six, she was the victim of type 3 FGM, an event she has described as "being engulfed in pain from head to toe".
Hibo Wardere: Every day for the next ten years, she sought answers from her mother, but was always denied a response.
Hibo Wardere: When Wardere was 16, she finally struck a deal with a relative, who promised to tell her everything about what happened after her wedding night.
Hibo Wardere: She was horrified by the revelations, and soon fled to London after the civil war broke out in the 1980s.

Hibo Wardere: Wardere's main ambition for the future is to see Female Genital Mutilation eradicated in her lifetime.
Hibo Wardere: Her memoir, "Cut", was published in April 2016.
